1.text:
The verse begins with the words In the Name of Allah. The reader starts the surah, and every reading of the Qurʾān, by calling on Allah. The phrase In the Name of Allah means that the action is done with His help, for His sake, and under His protection, so the one who begins admits that he cannot do anything by himself. The next words, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful, name Allah by two qualities of mercy. The first describes a kindness that reaches all of creation, and the second describes a mercy that is given most fully to those who believe. Together the two qualities show a God who gives generously and who gives in a lasting way. The verse is therefore more than a formula. It sets the tone for the whole surah, which is a prayer. Before the reader praises Allah in the next verse, he first remembers whose name he is speaking and whose mercy he is asking for. The next verse, All praise is for Allah, follows from this opening, because a person who begins by remembering the mercy of Allah is led to thank Him for it. Later in the surah the reader asks for guidance, and the opening is what makes that request come with mercy in view. A reader who begins in this way is reminded that the work he is about to do belongs to Allah from its first word to its last, and that he depends on that mercy at every step.

**What does the word Allah refer to?.**

The word 'Allah' refers to the Essence, and hence this name cannot be given to anyone except Allah. In short, Allah is the name of that Ultimate Reality which comprehends in Itself all the attributes of perfection, which is the creator and sustainer, unique and peerless. The word, 'Allah' is the greatest and the most comprehensive of the divine names. Hence, Allah mentioned several of His Names as Attributes for His Name Allah.

**Why does the surah begin with the Name?.**

The best way to begin any task is in the name of God, the Lord, the Being who is the source of all blessings, and whose blessings and mercy are continually pouring upon His creation. To commence any undertaking in His name is to pray that God, in His infinite mercy, should come to one’s assistance and bring one’s work to a successful conclusion. The two views can be brought into agreement with each other if we 'say that all the divine books share the common trait of beginning with the name of Allah, but the words Bismillah Al-Rahman Al-Rahim ‌ ‌ are peculiar to the Holy Qur'an, as is evident from certain Traditions (Ahadith) which report that in order to begin with the name of Allah anything he, undertook, the Holy Prophet used to say the words (Bismika Allahumma), but when the verse Bismillah Al-Rahman Al-Rahim ‌ ‌ was revealed, he adopted these words. The Holy Qur'an again and again instructs us to begin what we do with the name of Allah. By instructing man to begin everything with the name of Allah, Islam has given to the whole of his life an orientation towards Allah so that he may, with each step he takes, renew his allegiance to the covenant with Allah that nothing he does, not even his very being can come into existence without the will and the help of Allah. If not for the message and name of God in this world, how could it be the servant's home?

**Why are the names about mercy?.**

The Meaning of Ar-Rahman Ar-Rahim - the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim are two names derived from Ar-Rahmah (the mercy), but Rahman has more meanings that pertain to mercy than Ar-Rahim. These last two names of Allah are derived from the Arabic word raḥmah, which means mercy: proving the greatness and vastness of His Mercy and that His Mercy surrounds everything, and embraces all living beings. Every blessing is due to His mercy, and the believers receive the greatest mercy. It points to the fact that the creation of the heavens and the earth and the sustenance of the whole universe have no other motivation than making manifest Allah's quality of mercy. It is His own mercy which has required the creation and sustenance of the whole universal order.

**What do Rahman and Rahim signify?.**

Rahman ' signifies one whose mercy is common to all, and extends to the whole universe, to everything that will be created in the future. On the other hand, 'Rahim ' signifies one whose mercy is perfect in all possible ways. That is why 'Rahman ' is the exclusive attribute of Allah and the word is employed only when one is referring to Him. It is not permissible to qualify any created being as 'Rahman', for there cannot possibly be anyone else, beside Allah, whose mercy should be all-embracing and all-inclusive. (Tafsir al-Qurtubi) The signification of the word 'Rahim', on the contrary, does not contain anything which it should be impossible to find in a created being, for a man may be perfectly merciful in his dealings with another man.

**Why does the phrase have three words?.**

This phrase is composed of three words -- the Ietter 'Ba', 'Ism' and 'Allah'. The word 'Ism' has many lexical and intellectual nuances of meaning, the knowledge of which would not be essential for the average reader. It is sufficient to know that this word is translated in English as 'Name'. Thus, the phrase 'Bismillah' has these three respective significations according to the three connotations of the .preposition 'Ba' : But, in all the three forms, the phrase obviously remains incomplete unless one mentions the work which one intends to begin with the name of Allah or with its help or benediction.

**Why is Bismillah recited before the Qurʾān?.**

Bismillah is the First Ayah of Al-Fatihah The Companions started the Book of Allah with Bismillah: One should begin the recitation of the Qur'an by reciting both (I seek the protection of Allah) and, (Bismillahi: I begin with the name of Allah). And during the tilawah (the recitation of the Holy Qur'an) as well, saying AI 'Bismillah ... at the beginning of each Surah, except the Surah Al-Bara'ah (al-Taubah), is Sunnah. According to yet another hadith (Tradition), closing the door of one's house, putting out the lamp, covering a vessel, should all be done with the recitation of Bismillah.

2.text:
The verse states that all praise belongs to Allah. The phrase All praise is for Allah places praise at the start of the reader's words after the opening name. The word all means that no part of praise is kept back from Him, so whatever good the reader sees has its source in Allah. The phrase Lord of all worlds names Allah in His role as the one who nurtures and manages everything that exists. The word Lord points to care that brings a thing from its beginning toward its perfection, and the word worlds covers everything that exists, not only the human world. Together the two phrases link praise to a view of the whole universe. The one who praises Allah recognises that Allah alone is the source of every order, and that He is the one who sustains it. The verse follows the opening name in the first verse. Having named Allah with mercy, the reader now gives Him praise, since mercy is a reason for thanks. The next verse returns to the qualities of mercy, so the reader moves from praise to a closer view of the Lord of all worlds, who is also the Most Compassionate and the Most Merciful. This verse is the first step in the movement of the surah from the name, to praise, and then to worship and request. A reader who keeps the first verse in mind hears this verse as praise given for a mercy already named.

**What do praise and thanks mean?.**

" The Difference between Praise and Thanks Hamd is more general, in that it is a statement of praise for one's characteristics, or for what he has done. Thanks are given for what was done, not merely for characteristics. The Meaning of Al-Hamd Abu Jafar bin Jarir said, "The meaning of (Al-Hamdu Lillah) (all praise and thanks be to Allah) is: all thanks are due purely to Allah, alone, not any of the objects that are being worshipped instead of Him, nor any of His creation. When one proclaims, All thanks are due to Allah,' he will be thanking Him for His favors and bounties. " (mazhari) The Surah begins with the words Al-hamdulillah, signifying that all praise essentially belongs to Allah.

**What does praise to Allah express?.**

All praise belongs to Allah with regards to His essence, attributes and actions, because He is the Creator of everything. This is praise of the lovingly kind God, the Creator who provides daily provisions, the One in name and mark, the Lord who is found without seeking, recognized without being found, loved without being seen. In the perfection of His exaltedness, majesty, and holiness, He made them His deputies in laudation of Him, taught them how to praise Him, and gave them permission to do so. It is also said that laudation is Allah's because of His excessive blessings upon His servants whom He has guided to believe in Him. It is also said that (Lord of the worlds) means the Creator of all created beings, their Provider and the One Who changes them from one state into another.

**Why is the praise given to Allah alone?.**

Whosoever praises anything anywhere in the world is ultimately praising Allah. Admiring anything that exists in the created world is no more than showing one's admiration for a work of art or craft, which in fact is a praise of the artist or the craftsman. If there is only one Being in the whole universe who inherently deserves all praise, it necessarily follows from it that this Being alone should be Worthy of adoration and worship. When Allah alone is the ultimate cause for the nurture of the whole universe, He alone can, in reality, be worthy of praise.

**What does Lord of the worlds mean?.**

Lexically, the word, Rabb signifies 'one who nurtures'. And 'nurture' implies developing a thing by gradual stages in a manner which is conducive to its own good till it attains perfection. The word, Rabb is exclusive to the sacred Being of Allah, and cannot be employed in the case of any created being without adding some qualification, for a created being is itself in need of 'nurture', and cannot nurture anyone else. Al-'alamin is the plural of 'alam (world, universe, kingdom). "The worlds" include all possible forms of -- existence: the sky, the earth, the sun, the moon, stars, wind and rain, the angels, the jinns, animals, plants, minerals, and, of course, men. So, 'the Lord of all 'the worlds" means that Allah alone gives nurture to all the forms of existents that are to be found in this universe, or in the millions of universes that may lie beyond our own universe in the outer space.

**How does the Lord of the worlds connect to praise?.**

Seen in the light of this short phrase, 'Lord of the worlds', the universe reveals itself to be an incredibly complex, yet perfectly integrated order. ” (51:56) It may be said that the phrase 'the Lord of all the worlds' is in a way the proof of the claim made in the earlier phrase : Thus, the first verse of the Surah, as we said before, combines in itself the praise of Allah and a subtle indication of the first and basic principle of the Islamic creed -- the oneness of God.

**Why do the sources link praise with thanks?.**

All thanks and praise are due to Allah for these favors from beginning to end. All thanks and praise is due to Allah.' It was said that the statement, (All praise and thanks be to Allah), entails praising Allah by mentioning His most beautiful Names and most honorable Attributes. " The Difference between Praise and Thanks Hamd is more general, in that it is a statement of praise for one's characteristics, or for what he has done. Whosoever praises anything anywhere in the world is ultimately praising Allah.

3.text:
The verse repeats two names of Allah, the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful. The phrase the Most Compassionate, Most Merciful has two parts, one for a mercy that covers all creation and one for a mercy given most fully to believers. The verse is placed directly after the praise in the previous verse. Having named the Lord of all worlds as the one who gives praise its meaning, the surah now describes that Lord by the qualities of His mercy. The reader learns that the Lord who nurtures every creature is also the one who is merciful to them. The next verse names the Master of the Day of Judgment, so mercy is set beside justice and accountability. A reader who sees the mercy first is reminded that the account on that Day is also carried out by the One who is merciful. The repetition also gives the reader time to dwell on the mercy before moving on to the next name. The reader is asked to hold the two names together, since the first describes a mercy that is shown in the making and sustaining of all things, and the second describes a mercy that is shown in the guidance of believers.

**What do the two names of mercy describe?.**

The second verse speaks of the Divine quality of mercy, employing two adjectives Rahman and Rahim of which are hyperbolic terms in Arabic, and respectively connote the superabundance and perfection of Divine mercy. The reference to this particular attribute in this situation is perhaps intended to be a reminder of the fact that it is not through any external compulsion or inner need or any kind of necessity whatsoever that Allah has assumed the responsibility of nurturing the whole of His creation, but in response to the demand of His own quality of mercy. The Compassionate the Merciful that is to say the One who possesses ‘mercy’ which means to want what is good for those who deserve it. Allah said next, (Ar-Rahman (the Most Gracious), Ar-Rahim (the Most Merciful) We explained these Names in the Basmalah. Two names of Allah, Ar-Raḥmān and Ar-Raḥīm, derived from the word raḥmah, or mercy: indicating His mercy for creation, with the believers being the greatest recipients of it. When man looks at the world around him, he cannot fail to notice God’s power and mercy abundantly in evidence everywhere.

**Why are the names of mercy repeated?.**

Al-Qurtubi said, "Allah has described Himself by Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim' after saying the Lord of the Alamin', so His statement here includes a warning, and then an encouragement. The second verse speaks of the Divine quality of mercy, employing two adjectives Rahman and Rahim of which are hyperbolic terms in Arabic, and respectively connote the superabundance and perfection of Divine mercy. When man looks at the world around him, he cannot fail to notice God’s power and mercy abundantly in evidence everywhere. I have submitted to You and humbly seek Your help; have mercy on me.

**What does the Ever-Merciful add to the All-Merciful?.**

He is the All-Merciful inasmuch as He vivifies, the Ever-Merciful inasmuch as He displays. He is the All-Merciful who eases the road of wage-earning, the Ever-Merciful who lights up the candle of friendship in the road of the friends. He is the All-Merciful who gives the strivers the success of struggle, and the Ever-Merciful who gives the finders the realization of contemplation.

**What does the Divine mercy show about creation?.**

The second verse speaks of the Divine quality of mercy, employing two adjectives Rahman and Rahim of which are hyperbolic terms in Arabic, and respectively connote the superabundance and perfection of Divine mercy. Two names of Allah, Ar-Raḥmān and Ar-Raḥīm, derived from the word raḥmah, or mercy: indicating His mercy for creation, with the believers being the greatest recipients of it. When man looks at the world around him, he cannot fail to notice God’s power and mercy abundantly in evidence everywhere. If this whole universe did not exist, He would suffer no loss; if it does exist, it is no burden to Him.

4.text:
The verse describes Allah as the Master of the Day of Judgment. The phrase Master of the Day of Judgment names Allah as the one who has full authority on the Day when every person is repaid for what he did. The word master means the one who has possession and control of a matter, and the Day of Judgment is the Day when that control is seen clearly by all creatures. The verse follows the two names of mercy in the previous verse. The reader is given a balance between mercy and the account, so the mercy of Allah is not a reason to forget that every deed will be weighed. The next verse turns from the Master of that Day to the worship and the request of the servant. Since the Day is named here, the worship in the next verse is made with seriousness, and the prayer for guidance at the end of the surah is made with the Day in view. This verse links the mercy of Allah with His justice and turns the reader's thoughts toward accountability before he speaks to his Lord directly.

**What does Malik mean?.**

The word Malik has been derived from the root, 'milk' which signifies possessing a thing in such a manner that one has the right and power to dispose of it as one likes (See Qamus). Allah is Al-Malik (King or Owner) Allah is the True Owner (Malik) (of everything and everyone). ’ ‘God’s’ Q. 4016 if one reads it mālik as opposed to malik then this signifies that He has possession of the entire affair on the Day of Resurrection or else that He is ever described by this expression in the same way as He is described as ‘Forgiver of sin’ ghāfir al-dhanb.

**Why is the Day of Judgment mentioned specifically?.**

The reason for the specific mention of the Day of Judgement is that the mastery of none shall appear on that Day except that of God may He be exalted as is indicated by God’s words ‘Whose is the Kingdom today? Secondly, Allah being the Master, of everything even today as much as on the Day of Requital, why does this verse specifically mentions the Day of Requital? Indicating Sovereignty on the Day of Judgment Allah mentioned His sovereignty of the Day of Resurrection, but this does not negate His sovereignty over all other things.

**Who has the kingship on that Day?.**

But God's kingship is permanent, today and tomorrow, for it never comes to an end or disappears. This alludes to the permanence of the kingship of unity and the subsistence of the all-compel lingness of the divinity. In the two worlds nothing and no one is outside of His kingship and ruling power. For in the two worlds, ownership and kingship are God's, without associate, partner, requirement, or need. On that day God will ask “To whom belongs the Kingdom today?” [Sūrah Ghafir: 16] No one, no matter how high his status, will answer, and then God will reply Himself, “to God, the One, the Overcomer” [Sūrah Ghafir: 16].

**Who is the true owner on that Day?.**

Allah only mentioned the Day of Recompense here because on that Day, no one except Him will be able to claim ownership of anything whatsoever. Allah is Al-Malik (King or Owner) Allah is the True Owner (Malik) (of everything and everyone). Today He is the Lord of the Worlds and tomorrow the Owner of the Day of Doom, and none of the creatures is like this. (Owner of the Day of Judgement) the Arbitrator on the Day of Judgement which is the Day of Reckoning and settlement of disputes between created beings, i.e. the Day when people are judged according to their deeds; there is no judge save Him.

**What does the mastery of Allah exclude?.**

It should be obvious, on a little reflection, to everyone that the real master of every particle of dust in the universe can only be He who has created and nurtured it, Whose mastery over everything is complete, having neither a beginning nor an end, covering the living and the dead, the apparent and the hidden, the seen and the unseen. On the contrary, the mastery of man is delimited by a beginning and an end; it has a 'before' when it did not exist, and an 'after' when it will exist no more. Man's mastery and control extends to the living, not to the dead, to the seen, not to the unseen, to the external aspect of things, not to the internal. The real and complete mastery over everything, no doubt, belongs to Allah alone even in this world.

5.text:
The verse is addressed directly to Allah, and it turns the reader from praising Him to standing before Him. The phrase You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help has two halves joined by the word and. The first half means that worship is given to Allah and to Him alone. The word alone matters because it removes any other object from the act of worship. The second half means that help is asked from Allah and from Him alone. The reader is not only declaring worship, but also admitting that he cannot finish any task without Allah's help. The two halves come one after the other because worship is the purpose and help is the means that makes worship possible. The verse places You before we in each half. This puts Allah first in the sentence, so the words make clear that the one addressed is the one who deserves the worship. Looking back, the previous verses have named Allah, praised Him, and described His mercy and His authority on the Day of Judgment. This verse answers that description with a response. The reader stops describing and begins to speak to Allah in the first person plural, joining the community of believers. Looking ahead, the next verse asks for guidance on the straight path, and that request depends on the admission made here. A servant who admits that he worships Allah alone and asks Him for help is ready to ask for the right path. The verse is therefore the point where the surah moves from praise to prayer.

**What does worship alone mean?.**

You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help that is to say we reserve worship for You alone by way of acknowledging Your Oneness tawhīd and so on and we ask for Your assistance in worship and in other things. The Merit of stating the Object of the Action before the Doer of the Act, and the Merit of these Negations "You...", means, we worship You alone and none else, and rely on You alone and none else. We worship and obey none except You; we associate no one with You, and from You alone do we ask for help in all our affairs. It is to keep oneself adorned with a worship that has no eye-service and an obedience that has no hypocrisy.

**Why is help sought from Allah alone?.**

We worship and obey none except You; we associate no one with You, and from You alone do we ask for help in all our affairs. I have submitted to You and humbly seek Your help; have mercy on me. (Thee (alone) we worship), we turn to you as the only One God and we obey you; ((Thee alone) we ask for help), we ask for your help in worshipping You and from You we obtain confidence in obeying You. Hence the phrase (to You alone we pray for help). (to You alone we pray for help) does not mention the purpose for which help is being sought.

**Why is worship named before asking for help?.**

The Merit of stating the Object of the Action before the Doer of the Act, and the Merit of these Negations "You...", means, we worship You alone and none else, and rely on You alone and none else. This is because after the servant praised and thanked Allah, he stands before Him, addressing Him directly; (You we worship, and You we ask for help from). The fourth verse : “You alone we worship, and from You alone we seek help” has a double aspect, one of praise and another of prayer. The three verses having made it clear that man is totally and absolutely dependent on Allah in all the three states of his life, it logically and naturally leads to the conclusion that Allah alone is worthy of being worshipped, for in Arabic the word ibadah (worship) connotes showing the utmost humility and submissiveness out of an intense respect and love for someone, and such an attitude of willing self-abasement cannot justly be adopted towards anyone except Allah.

**What does worship include?.**

It teaches man not to worship anyone except Allah, not to consider anyone else as being really capable of satisfying his needs, and not to beg anyone else to satisfy these needs. According to most of the commentators, it generalizes the idea of the request to cover everything from acts of worship to all possible worldly or other-worldly concerns. Then, acts of worship (Ibadah) are not limited merely to prescribed prayers or fasting. Imam al-Ghazzali in his book Arba'in has enumerated ten forms which worship can take:- 1. Encouraging the Performance of the Acts of Worship during Times of Distress Allah also recommended that His Prophet resort to acts of worship during times when he felt distressed because of the disbelievers who defied and denied him.

**What does the verse show about the servant?.**

Allah called His Prophet an Abd Allah called His Messenger an Abd (servant) when He mentioned sending down His Book, the Prophet's involvement in inviting to Him, and when mentioning the Isra' (overnight journey from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis and then to heaven), and these are the Prophet's most honorable missions. Allah said, (All praise and thanks be to Allah, Who has sent down to His servant (Muhammad) the Book (the Qur'an) (18:1), (And when the servant of Allah (Muhammad) stood up invoking Him (his Lord Allah in prayer), (72:19) and, (Glorified (and Exalted) be He (Allah) (above all that they associate with Him) Who took His servant (Muhammad) for a journey by night) (17:1). ’ God requires His servant to live his life with such feelings and emotions. This is because after the servant praised and thanked Allah, he stands before Him, addressing Him directly; (You we worship, and You we ask for help from).

**Why is the straight path requested after this?.**

(Guide us to the straight path.) This method is more appropriate and efficient in bringing about a positive answer to the pleas, and this is why Allah recommended this better method. Lord, show us the path that is, to You, the true path. Enable us to tread the path of Your chosen servants. Help us to avoid the path of those who have gone astray, and the path of those who have incurred Your wrath due to their obstinacy.

6.text:
The prayer is a request to be led. “Guide us along the Straight Path” is the whole wording of this verse. It is a prayer for people together, not an account that someone has already reached the end. “Us” leaves the speaker among other people, so the request asks that all be led, not one person only. To guide is more than to point out a direction. It is to lead toward the right end, to show the way, and to help the traveller stay on it. The request asks for knowledge of the way and help in following it. “along the Straight Path” gives the direction a name. “Straight” marks a way without crookedness, a clear path that does not turn away from its end. The image is not simply of reaching a place once, but of following a course. A person can know a path and still need to be kept firm upon it, so the prayer asks for guidance again. The previous verses have praised Allah and turned that praise into worship and a request for help. Now that plea becomes specific: help is asked for in the form of guidance, not for a named worldly gain. The next verse describes the Straight Path by naming those who have received blessing and by contrasting them with two other groups. That description completes the request here. The reader first asks to be led, then asks for a way shaped by good company and separated from error. Read together, the two verses make guidance a continuing need, not a claim that one has already arrived.

**What “Guide us” means.**

Show and facilitate for us the right way, the path of submission to You which has no crookedness, and make us firm upon it –. (Guide us to the straight path) guide us to the established Religion that You are pleased with, i.e. In other words, Allah Himself, in His great mercy, has taught man what to pray for: “Guide us in the straight path, the path of those on whom You have bestowed Your grace, not of those who have incurred Your wrath, nor of those who have gone astray. Also, (And shown him the two ways (good and evil) (90:10), means, We explained to him the paths of good and evil.' Also, Allah said, (He (Allah) chose him (as an intimate friend) and guided him to a straight path) (16:121), and, (And lead them on to the way of flaming Fire (Hell) (37:23).

**Why people already guided still ask.**

The teaching with regard to the prayer for being guided in the straight path is addressed equally to all men or all Muslims and to saints and prophets who have already received guidance and are even a source of guidance for other men. To sum up, the Qur'anic prayer (guide us in the straight path) is most comprehensive, and certainly, one of the most important prayers taught to man. " In this verse, the faithful ask for all three of these from God, for not everyone who sees the road travels the road, and not everyone who travels the road reaches the destination. Many there are who hear but do not see, many there are who see but do not recognize, and many there are who recognize but do not find. Therefore, in this Ayah Allah commanded the believers to believe, and this command is not redundant since what is sought here is firmness and continuity of performing the deeds that help one remain on the path of faith.

**What the Straight Path means.**

It is also said that this means: make us firm in holding fast to it. It is also said that the straight path refers to Allah's Book, and guidance to this means guidance to that which it prescribes as lawful or unlawful and to the exposition of its content. Hence the Arabs would describe the honest person as being straight and the wicked person as being crooked. Similarly, Allah said, (And verily, you (O Muhammad) are indeed guiding (mankind) to the straight path) (42:52), and, (All praise and thanks be to Allah, Who has guided us to this) (7:43), meaning, guided us and directed us and qualified us for this end - Paradise. It is seeking straightness and firm fixity in the religion. The Holy Qur'an itself gives us the promise of such increase: “As for those who follow the straight path, Allah will increase their guidance.

**How the path is followed.**

"Lead us to this path, make us travel upon it, and make us firm in it. " The faithful are saying, "O God, show us Your road, then make us go forth on the road, then take us from traveling to being pulled. Enable us to tread the path of Your chosen servants. Help us to avoid the path of those who have gone astray, and the path of those who have incurred Your wrath due to their obstinacy. Hence, (Guide us to the straight way) means, "Make us firm on the path of guidance and do not allow us to deviate from it."

**The degrees of guidance.**

The Third Degree of guidance The third degree of guidance is still more particular, being special to true believers (Muminin) and the God-fearing (Muttaqin). Like the first degree, the third kind of guidance too descends directly to the individual from Allah, and it is called, Tawfiq That is to say, Allah's grace provides a man with internal and external means and circumstances which should make it easy, and even pleasant for him to accept and act upon the guidance of the Holy Quran, and difficult to ignore or oppose it. The servant needs Allah the Exalted every hour of his life to help him remain firm on the path of guidance and to make him even more firm and persistent on it. Therefore, Allah directed the servant to invoke Him constantly, so that He provides him with His aid and with firmness and success.

**Why guidance is needed by everyone.**

A Cumulative view of guidance Keeping in mind the three distinct degrees of guidance, one can easily see that guidance is a thing which everyone does possess in some way, and yet no one, not even the greatest, can do without wishing to attain more of its advanced and higher stages. Hence, of all the prayers man can address to Allah, the most important is the prayer for guidance, which has been taught to us in the very first Surah of the Holy Qur'an; and this prayer is as necessary for the greatest of prophets and men of Allah as for an ordinary Muslim. Many a tavern-goer has saddled up a lion! [DS 110] Concerning His words, "Guide us," it has been said, "Cut off our secret cores from witnessing the others, display in our hearts the dawning lights, isolate our intentions from the defilement of traces, take us beyond the way stations of seeking and inference to the courtyards of proximity and union, prevent us from taking repose in likenesses and shapes by treating us with the gentleness of finding union, and unveil to us thereby the witnessing of majesty and beauty."

7.text:
“the Path of those You have blessed” completes the request for the Straight Path in the verse before it. “The Path” takes that request and gives it a human shape: it is a way people can follow, not a bare direction without an example. “Of those You have blessed” points to people whose good comes from a blessing they received, rather than from a claim they make about themselves. The prayer asks to be placed with them and to follow the way they follow. The next phrase, “not those You are displeased with”, marks a path that is to be avoided. It is set against the people who received blessing, so the reader is not asking only for a name or a label, but for a way of living. “or those who are astray” marks a second refusal. Both endings are outside the path sought, but the wording keeps them as two descriptions rather than blending them into one. The whole line therefore has a positive request followed by two boundaries: ask for the way of the blessed, and do not take either of the other ways. The phrase joins the prayer to the verses before it. After praise, worship, help, and the request for guidance, this verse states what kind of path the prayer means here. The reader asks for guidance in this life by turning toward people who were blessed and away from those described by displeasure or being astray again.

**Who is on the blessed path.**

This verse, then, determines the straight path in a positive manner, identifying it with the path followed by men of these four categories. Allah's statement, (Not (the way) of those who earned Your anger, nor of those who went astray) meaning guide us to the straight path, the path of those upon whom you have bestowed Your grace, that is, the people of guidance, sincerity and obedience to Allah and His Messengers. (The path of those whom Thou hast favoured), the Religion of those whom You have blessed with the Religion and who are the followers of Moses, before the blessings of Allah deserted them, in that He shaded them with a white cloud and sent down on them honey and quails when they were in the wilderness. It is also said that (the path of those whom Thou hast favoured) refers to the prophets. The same path as those of Your creation whom You have blessed with guidance, such as the prophets, the truthful, martyrs, and the righteous ones.

**Those who incur wrath or go astray.**

the path of those whom You have favoured with guidance from alladhīna together with its relative clause is substituted by ghayri l-maghdūbi ‘alayhim not the path of those against whom there is wrath namely the Jews and nor of those who are astray namely the Christians. ” Those who have incurred Allah's wrath are the people, who inspite of being quite familiar with the commandments of Allah willfully go against them out of a calculated perversity or in the service of their desires, or, in other words, who are deficient in obeying divine injunctions. But, help us to avoid the path of those whom Allah is angry with, whose intentions are corrupt, who know the truth, yet deviate from it. Also, help us avoid the path of those who were led astray, who lost the true knowledge and, as a result, are wandering in misguidance, unable to find the correct path. Keep us away from the path of those who earned Your anger, who knew the truth and did not follow it – as was the case with the Israelites; and keep us away from the path of those who lost their way and were not guided, because they were neglectful in seeking the Truth and being guided by it – as was the case with the Christians.

**The path and the need for guidance.**

In defining the straight path too, He has also enumerated those of His servants who find special favor with Him -- all of which argues that, in trying to understand the Book of Allah and to act upon it, one cannot solely rely on one's own study and judgment, but must turn to someone who knows. In view of the need for the straight path in worldly and other worldly concerns both, this is the prayer which should constantly be on the lips and in the heart of a true Muslim -- never as an empty verbal exercise, but with a sincere intention and with the meaning of the words fully present in the mind. For instance, Allah said, (He whom Allah guides, he is the rightly-guided; but he whom He sends astray, for him you will find no Wali (guiding friend) to lead him (to the right path) (18:17) and, (Whomsoever Allah sends astray, none can guide him; and He lets them wander blindly in their transgression) (7:186). Help us to avoid the path of those who have gone astray, and the path of those who have incurred Your wrath due to their obstinacy. The path of those whom Thou hast blessed, not of those who incur wrath, nor of the misguided.

**Anger, rejection, and error.**

(Not of those who earn Thine anger), not the religion of the Jews who earned Your anger, whom You forsook and whose hearts You did not protect until they became complaisant. (Nor of those who go astray), nor the religion of the Christians who erred from Islam. Thus, the essential meaning of the verse is that, in praying for the straight path, we do not ask for the path of those who are the slaves of their desires, perverse in thought and action, and deficient in performing their religious obligations, nor the path of those who are ignorant or unmindful or misled, and indulge in excess and exaggeration in religious matters, but wish for a path between these two extremes, which inclines neither towards excess nor towards deficiency, and which is as free of the promptings of desires as of doubts and confusions and of erroneous beliefs. If one associates somebody else with Allah in this respect and, in spite of being familiar with the divine injunctions regarding what is permissible (halal) and what is forbidden (haram), goes against them, believing that someone other than Allah too can demand obedience in these matters, one is virtually worshipping him and being guilty of the sin of association (shirk). Those who know, but avoid implementing the truth, deserve the anger, unlike those who are ignorant. We should also mention that both the Christians and the Jews have earned the anger and are led astray, but the anger is one of the attributes more particular of the Jews.
